newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM vows to slow military spending, cut deficit.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM vows to slow military spending, cut deficit.

text.p: New Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh said on Thursday he would uphold strict monetary discipline and help cut the wide national current account deficit by slowing down military expenditure.

Chavalit, who is also defence minister, said his government would shelve a plan by the navy to buy two submarines worth 17 billion baht ($680 million) and a military project to launch a $1.04 billion spy satellite and communications system.

"I already said that since we are facing the problem of a current account deficit, the submarine and satellite system can be slowed down," he told parliament during a debate on his week-old government's policy statement.

"The military has pulled back so much, compared to our neighbours like Malaysia and Singapore which spend about five to six percent of their gross domestic product (GDP) for military expenses," said Chavalit, who was also defence minister in the previous government.
"The Thai military during my tenure spent only 2.5 percent of GDP," he said in reply to charges made by the opposition that he planned to spend heavily on a military build up.

Thailand's 1995 current account deficit at 8.1 percent of GDP was one of the highest in the region, according to analysts. The central bank projects this would expand up to 8.3 percent of GDP in 1996.
The new government is required by law to declare its policy at a joint session of parliament for acknowledgement. The session will end late Thursday.
The opposition also challenged Chavalit to use his influence with Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) to help overcome human rights abuses in that country.
The premier said that although he had close ties with the SLORC he could not dictate domestic policy to them.

For most of the day, the opposition and some senators attacked the new government's policy statement, saying it recognised national economic woes such as a slowing economy and sluggish exports, but lacked details.
The policy statement, outlined by Chavalit in parliament on Wednesday, targeted resuscitation of the ailing economy and political reform as its key objectives.
Chavalit's took power after polls last month
